name: Scottish English (Scottish Standard English and Scots)
summary: Scottish English is a continuum from Scottish Standard English (SSE: professional-class, standard grammar, Scottish accent) to broad Scots (a related language with its own words and grammar). For an actor the safest layers are: (1) sound features of SSE (rhotic r, /hw/ in 'which', pull=pool, Scottish Vowel Length Rule, monophthong FACE/GOAT, no TRAP/BATH split); (2) a few Scots words and the -nae negatives (dinnae, cannae, isnae), checked in the Dictionary of the Scots Language (DSL, Scottish National Dictionary); (3) 'ken' as 'know' and as a discourse tag. Round 2 verified ken, dinnae/cannae, outwith, wean, bairn and glaikit in DSL, Scots grammar items in an Open University Scots course, 'needs washed' on the Yale Grammatical Diversity Project, and Glasgow consonant change in the University of Glasgow STELLA report. Removed or demoted: 'provost' (a civic title, irrelevant to acting) and formal/legal words (depute, interdict etc.); 'och' is left out (not confirmed in a dictionary entry and a stereotype when paired as 'och aye'). Region matters: Glasgow, Edinburgh, North-East (Doric), Highlands, Shetland differ.

grammar.dialect: -nae negatives: dinnae, cannae, didnae, isnae, wisnae (-na in the North-East and Shetland)
grammar.condition: DSL (SND) records -na as the unstressed enclitic 'not' with auxiliaries (canna, dinna, haena, winna; first recorded in 1588), with -nae forms: dinnae (Sc. 1994), cannae (Sc. 1893), disnae (w.Lth. 2000). OpenLearn: -nae in West Central and East Central South, -na in the North-East and Shetland. Broad-Scots register; SSE speakers use not/n't.
grammar.example_standard: I don't know. / She can't stop here.
grammar.example_dialect: I dinnae know. / She cannae stop here.

pronunciation.rule: Rhoticity: Scottish English is mostly rhotic; /r/ is pronounced after vowels. Realisations: approximant, tap (flap), or a now rare trill. Some Edinburgh and Glasgow speakers are non-rhotic, especially working-class youth in reports (sources 1, 13).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Pronounce every r in 'car', 'hard', 'bird'. A light tap is more natural than a heavy trill.

pronunciation.rule: wh / w distinction: 'which' /hw/ vs 'witch' /w/ in many speakers.
pronunciation.actor_tip: A small puff of air before the w in 'which', 'whale'.

pronunciation.rule: Scottish Vowel Length Rule (Aitken's Law): vowels are long before voiced fricatives, before /r/ and at morpheme boundaries; short before voiceless sounds. It also splits PRICE into short [ʌi, ai] and long [aˑe, ɑːe] ('side' vs 'sighed').
pronunciation.ipa: [seːv] save vs [sef] safe; [tiːð] teethe vs [tiθ] teeth; need vs kneed
pronunciation.actor_tip: Lengthen the vowel before v, z, th (as in 'this'), r. It is duration, not emphasis. Weaker in Northern Scots and Shetland.

pronunciation.rule: Pull-pool merger: Scottish English has no /ʊ/; it uses /u/ so pull = pool, full = fool.
TRAP-BATH-PALM merger: most varieties have no /æ/-/ɑː/ split; 'bath', 'trap', 'palm' share the same vowel.
cot-caught merger in most Central Scots varieties: 'cot' and 'caught' are the same.
FACE and GOAT are monophthongs in most varieties: [e] and [o~oʊ].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Hold the vowel steady in 'day', 'go', 'home'; no glide to 'ee' or 'oo'.

pronunciation.rule: Loch sound: the ch in 'loch' is a voiceless velar fricative /x/ in words that have it.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Soft throat-clearing 'kh'; only in loch-type words, not 'church'.

pronunciation.rule: Glottal stop for t: in some colloquial speech /t/ after a vowel becomes [ʔ] ('butter' [ˈbʌʔər]). Glasgow is described as the possible home of the glottal stop; it is increasing in Glasgow as a traditional feature reinforced (STELLA report).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Use mainly for casual urban (Glasgow) characters: 'bu'er', 'wa'er'.

pronunciation.rule: th in Glasgow: traditional [h] for th (debuccalised, 'something' ~ 'somehing'); th-fronting [f] ('think' ~ 'fink') has been reported since the early 1980s and is spreading in working-class youth speech but is not traditional (STELLA report).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Use only for Glasgow working-class characters; don't use for Edinburgh or SSE speakers.

pronunciation.rule: L is mostly dark (velarised) in Scottish English; 'glen' is an exception.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Pull the back of the tongue up for l.

intonation.rule: No pitch-contour description for Scottish English was verified in the opened sources. What can be used is RHYTHM: the Scottish Vowel Length Rule gives vowel duration that depends on the following sound, not on stress, so word rhythm differs from English (source 2).
intonation.actor_tip: Time long and short vowels by the sound that follows them, not by emphasis.

common_mistakes: Putting 'och', 'aye', 'ken', 'dinnae' and 'wee' in every line. Use one or two per monologue.
'Och aye the noo' and other stage-Scotland phrases. Stereotype; not used.
Using the Braveheart/Highland accent for a Glasgow or Edinburgh character. Regional differences are large.
Rolling the r heavily in every word. It is rhotic, not trilled.
Giving the Scottish Vowel Length Rule a drawl. It is duration set by the next sound, not emphasis.
Using Scots grammar (nivver, -it past, 'A seen') for a professional or formal character. SSE is the formal variety.
Using th-fronting or glottal stops for every Scottish character. These are mostly Glasgow/urban working-class.
Using 'provost' and similar formal civic words in ordinary dialogue.
Writing eye-dialect ('dinna ken', 'aboot', 'oot'). Use light word choices and standard spelling; carry the sounds in notes.
generational_notes: Source 1/3: Scots is the informal end and SSE the formal end of a continuum; many speakers switch.

Glasgow: th-fronting is a newer feature reported since the early 1980s; the glottal stop is described as a traditional feature that is strengthening; r-lessness in youth speech is a loss of a traditional Scottish feature (STELLA report, source 13).
The SND date ranges show wean (1725-2000), glaikit (1706-2003), ken (1710-2005) as long-lived, but the dictionary gives no age-by-age usage.
Aitken's Law is applied less consistently in Northern Scots and Shetland (source 2).
Specific age data for Scots vocabulary use was not found.
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first; add Scottish flavour in layers.
Step 1: decide register and place. Professional/formal = SSE (standard grammar + accent only). Informal/working-class = a few Scots words. Glasgow/West and Edinburgh/East differ.
Step 2 (sound notes): rhotic r, pull=pool, monophthong FACE/GOAT, vowel length rule, /hw/ for wh-words.
Step 3 (grammar): choose at most two: -nae negatives (dinnae, cannae, isnae), 'needs washed', 'wait on', 'I'm wanting'. Add 'ye ken' as a tag only for casual speech.
Step 4 (vocabulary): one or two of aye, wee, wean (West) or bairn, braw, bonnie, numpty. Do not add 'och aye'.
No eye-dialect (aboot, oot, wis). No 'provost' or legal vocabulary.
Glasgow working-class youth: glottal stop and th-fronting only in sound notes.
In actor notes, state the register (SSE / Scots) and region.

open_questions: 'wee', 'aye' and 'och' have no opened DSL entry: the DSL pages for 'wee' and 'aye' returned a source-file error. They rest on Wikipedia only. 'Och' is left out; 'och aye the noo' is a stereotype (seen in a search result, not opened).
Intonation: no pitch description verified (the Wells UCL lecture PDF and Hirst's UK declarative rises paper could not be read). Glasgow/Edinburgh rise or fall patterns are open.
The Glasgow th-fronting and glottal-stop claims come from a STELLA annex that is summarised from research; frequency by age/class was not checked.
Edinburgh non-rhotic speakers: reported in source 1/13; status today not checked.
Highland English features (Gaelic influence) not verified beyond one sentence.
The DSL wean entry is from the 1700+ dictionary; it gives no modern frequency. Region split (wean West, bairn East/North) is directional, not quantitative.
After-perfect ('He is after going') is listed for Scotland in source 1 and in YGDP, but frequency in everyday Scottish English is unclear; treated as low.
Whether 'needs washed' is general Scots, SSE or only some regions was not checked beyond YGDP and source 1.

sub_regions.name: 글래스고 vs 에든버러
sub_regions.note: 글래스고: 성문음 t(오랜 전통이 강화되는 중), 노동계층 청소년의 th-fronting과 r 약화(출처 13). 에든버러: 비-rhotic 변이가 언급됨(출처 1). 단어 wean은 서부 중심, bairn은 더 넓게 쓰임(출처 8, 9).

sub_regions.note: SSE는 전문직 계층의 표준 스코틀랜드 영어, Scots는 별개 언어에 가까운 연속체의 한쪽 끝(출처 1, 3). 인물의 계층·장면에 맞춰 선택.

confidence_detail: medium-high for -nae negatives, ken, outwith, wean, bairn, glaikit (DSL entries opened); medium for grammar and regional items (OpenLearn, YGDP); medium for sounds (Wikipedia); low for intonation (nothing verified) and for Highland English.
